text: Build a class with two calls. Add num adds a number from a stream. Find median returns the median of everything added so far. If the count is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — numbers come one at a time, and I can be asked for the median at any point. So I never see the whole list up front. Is that right? And the key thing: I don't need the list sorted. I only need the one or two middle values. If I split the numbers into a smaller half and a bigger half, the median is just the top of one half, or the average of both tops.
Yes, that's right. And duplicates are allowed.
Will find median ever be called on an empty stream? Are there any constraints on the input size?
Values are between minus ten to the fifth and ten to the fifth. At most fifty thousand calls in total. Find median is only called after at least one add num.

OK. So two values add up to at most two hundred thousand in size. That fits in an int, but I'll still be careful when I average them. Let me run through the example. Add one, add two: the median is one plus two, over two, which is one point five. Add three: now it's one, two, three, so the median is two. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to keep a vector, and sort a copy on every find median. That's n log n per query — at fifty thousand calls it takes over a minute. Way too slow. A better naive way keeps the vector sorted and inserts in place. Finding the spot is log n, but shifting is linear, so it's quadratic overall and won't scale. This problem reminds me of the classic two heaps pattern. A max-heap holds the smaller half, so its top is the biggest of the small numbers. A min-heap holds the bigger half, so its top is the smallest of the big numbers. Those two tops are exactly the middle. Each add is log n, and each median is constant time.

Here's the plan. One: a max-heap for the smaller half, a min-heap for the bigger half. Two: after every add, the max-heap has the same size or one more, and its top is no bigger than the min-heap's top. Three: odd count, return the max-heap top; even count, average both tops, casting first. One thing worth flagging — there are two rules, not one. A big number in the small half keeps the sizes fine but breaks the tops. So every add must fix both size and order. There's a trade-off here. I can pick the heap by size and then fix the order, or always route the number through both heaps. The first usually does less work; the second is shorter and easier to prove. I'll write mine first, then the clean one. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Mine picks the heap by size, then fixes the order with one swap. Ties go to the max-heap, because of the less-or-equal check, so it's always the same size or one bigger — that's why the odd case reads its top. One thing worth flagging — why is one swap enough? Before this add, both rules held. Only the new number can be in the wrong half, and the swap moves one value each way, so the sizes stay the same and the order holds again. No loop needed. Also, the not-empty check on the min-heap is required: on the very first add it's empty, and calling top on it is undefined behavior.
Works. Can you make it shorter?

Clean always pushes into the small half, passes its top to the big half, then rebalances by size. Let me walk through that. After the push, the top of lo is the biggest of the small side plus the new number, so moving it to hi keeps the order rule for free. Then, if hi got bigger, I move its smallest back. Both rules hold with no comparison at all. One thing worth flagging — the cast. Here I turn one top into a double before the add. If I add two ints first and cast after, that's safe with this problem's range, but int max plus int max would overflow to minus one. Casting first gives the right answer.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Stream five, two, eight, nine, one, four; expected medians five, three point five, five, six point five, five, four point five. In Mine, the last row is the key one. Four goes to the min-heap, but now the max-heap top is five and the min-heap top is four — out of order. One swap moves five up and four down, sizes stay three and three, and the median is four point five. In Clean, look at add eight: it goes into lo, straight up to hi, and since hi now has two and lo one, five comes back down. Same medians, every step. Corner cases: integer division turns two, one into one instead of one point five. With no swap, two, one passes by luck, but two, one, one gives two instead of one. Greater-or-equal in the swap check is harmless.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is log n per add num, since each one does a constant number of heap pushes and pops. Find median is constant time; it only reads tops. The space complexity is linear — every number is stored once. In the worst-case scenario the constants differ. Over fifty thousand adds, Clean always does a hundred twenty-five thousand pushes. Mine does about a hundred thousand on random or sorted input, but a stream that alternates big and small forces a swap on every add — about a hundred fifty thousand. Oh, one more thing — if all numbers were between zero and a hundred, I'd skip heaps and keep a counting array of a hundred and one slots, then walk it to find the middle.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named two invariants, size and order, and showed why size alone isn't enough. You proved one swap is enough, because sizes stay the same and only the new number can be misplaced. And you caught the overflow in the average, casting before the add. Good work.
